lawyer:
Md Shamsul Huq, Assistant Attorney-General -For the Appellant
Mahbubur Rahman with Emdadul Huq Kazi, Advocates -For the Respondents
parties:
Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Dhaka ------ Appellant
Vs.
M.M.M. Electrical Industry Ltd. and ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: This appeal filed under section 196-D of the Customs Act 1969 is against the judgment and order dated 18-2-2001 passed by the Customs, Excise and Vat Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka in Nothi No. CEVT/Case (Cus)-151 /2000 dated 18-2-2001. 

 2. The respondent No.1 imported 600 pieces of three phase Electronic Energy Meter and after arrival of the goods submitted Bill of Entry on 15-2-2000 and at the time of submission of the Bill of Entry the respondents declared the customs duties and other charges on the basis of S.R.O. No. 125 dated 19-6-99 as a result of which duties and other charges were paid but in fact the consignment ought to have been assessed pursuant to S.R.O. No. 126 dated 10-6-99 where under customs duties are livable at the rate of 5% and no VAT was livable at the time when the goods were declared on 1-1-2001. The goods were released on payment of customs duties and other charges on the basis of S.R.O. No. 125 dated 19-6-99. When this mistake was detected by the respondent No.1 importer they filed an application on 21-5-2000 claiming refund of the excess duties and other charges as paid at the time of release of the goods. It appears that thereafter another application was filed by the respondent No.1 on 23-6-2000 stating that they were not aware of the S.R.O. No. 126 dated 10-6-99 therefore, they made an excess payment. Appellant however, by his order dated 3-12-2001 disposed of both the applications and refused to refund the amount on the sole ground that at the time of making payment of customs duties it was paid by the respondent No.1 voluntarily and therefore, it is not a case of inadvertence or misconstruction of law and at the time of payment of customs duties and other charges the respondent-importer did not raise any objection nor made the payment on protest. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order, the respondent No.1 filed an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal by the impugned order dated 18-2-2001 allowed the appeal which is under challenge in this appeal. 

 3. Mr. Shamsul Huq, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the appellant, submits that the respondent No. 2 without considering the materials on record allowed the appeal of the respondent No. 1 which does not come within the ambit of section 33 of the Customs Act inasmuch as the cargo imported by the respondent No. 1 was attracted by the S.R.O. No. 125 dated 19-6-99 and not by S.R.O. No. 126 dated 10-6-99. The learned Assistant Attorney-General then submits that the tribunal committed illegality in allowing the appeal in that they have failed to notice the fact that no objection was raised by the respondent No. 1 at the time of payment of customs duties and other charges. The learned Assistant Attorney-General further submits that the impugned decision is not based on the materials on record as the payment was not made inadvertently or on misconstruction of law and consequently, the impugned order is liable to be set aside. 

 4. Mr. Mahbubur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 1, on the other hand, submits that there is no dispute in this case that the consignments imported by the respondent No.1 are covered by S.R.O. No. 126 dated 10-6-99 but mistakenly the respondent No.1 declared the consignment under S.R.O. No. 125 dated 19-6-99 and refund was denied of the excess amount paid by the respondent No.1, though the first application was filed on 21-1-2000 as soon as the mistake was detected by the respondent No.1 and that application was well within the period of limitation as prescribed by section 33 of the Customs Act, but the appellant rejected that application on the sole ground that the payment was made without any objection therefore, it is not covered by section 33 of the Customs Act. The learned Advocate further submits that the appellant refused to refund the excess amount on the ground that it is not a case of inadvertent error or misconstruction of law but it is contended by him that it is evident from the materials that the payment was made due to inadvertent error as at that time they were not aware of the S.R.O. No. 126 dated 16-6-99 and therefore, in the facts and circumstances of the case there was no occasion for the respondent No. 1 to raise any objection or to make the payment under protest as the payment was made on mistaken idea. The learned Advocate further submits that the correct view of law is that there is no such provision in section 33 or in any of the sections of the Customs Act that if excess payment of customs duties is made at the time of releasing the goods it had to be made on protest and section 33 contemplates that if any payment is made due to inadvertent error or misconstruction of law, the importer is entitled to claim the refund of the said amount within 6(six) months from the date of payment and in this case the payment was made on 27-2-2000 and both the applications were filed by the respondent No.1 within time and thus the Tribunal taking a correct view of law and facts rightly set aside the order of the Commissioner of Customs. 

 5. We have examined the materials on record and considered the submissions made by the learned Advocates for the respective parties. It appears that the Commissioner of Customs taking an erroneous view of law and facts, illegally rejected the application of the respondent No. 1 dated 21-5-2000 and 23-6-2000 on the sole ground that at the time of making the payment of customs duties and other charges it was not made on protest. From the materials on record and the observation of the Appellate Tribunal made in the impugned judgment it appears that the respondent No.1 has been able to make out a case under section 33 of the Customs Act and there is nothing in the section to indicate that it is only in case of payment on protest by the importer that the refund can be made. It further appears that in the aforesaid applications dated 21-5-2000 and 23-6-2000 the respondent No. 1 made out a case of inadvertent error, which resulted in excess payment. Moreover, the admitted position is that the consignment in question is governed by S.R.O. No. 126 dated 10-6-99. Therefore, the Tribunal rightly allowed the appeal and directed the appellant to refund the excess customs duties and other charges paid by the respondent No.1 at the time of releasing the goods.
